cc953fab586ee2b1f5882c32.title_original: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
cc953fab586ee2b1f5882c32.excerpt: arXiv:2611.30483v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was unin

28a643a41fb0b76aef3676ea.title_original: Queuing for Secrets: Model-Based Remote Timing Attacks
28a643a41fb0b76aef3676ea.excerpt: arXiv:2611.30513v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Remote timing attacks exploit variations in response times to infer sensitive information about remote systems. Their effectiveness, however, is often limited by the difficulty of accurately modeling the stochastic nature of server-side response times, taking into account the intrinsic variability of the service time of a request and the impact of varying workloads on the observed response times. In this article, we propose a new stochastic framework for remote timing attacks based on queuing models and Bayesian statistics. We assume that the attacker knows the service time distributions of two classes of requests and that the information leakage occurs when a malicious observer can distinguish with high probability the class based on the observed response times in the presence of noise induced by exogenous workload. Our experimental evaluation on popular websites demonstrates the practical viability of the approach: our attack outperforms formal techniques based on deterministic service times and existing empirical techniques, while requiring less tuning and fewer hyper-parameters compared to previous formal approaches. Overall, our results show that principled stochastic modeling can provide a solid foundation for building more effective remote timing attacks under realistic network and workload conditions.

9efa85a218f4e6226dc0a772.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31208v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $\Theta\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.

1d90872e349a1311e549f9c5.title_original: VideoMark: A Distortion-Free Robust Watermarking Framework for Video Diffusion Models
1d90872e349a1311e549f9c5.excerpt: arXiv:2504.16359v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work presents VideoMark, a training-free watermarking framework for video diffusion models with frame-aligned 2D VAEs. VideoMark embeds pseudorandom error-correcting (PRC) codewords by modulating the signs of Gaussian initialization noise without model retraining. Under a joint pseudorandomness assumption on the instantiated PRC encoder, the resulting initialization tensor is computationally indistinguishable from the Gaussian reference; exact distributional equality holds for the ideal independent uniform-sign construction. To support temporally structured video watermarking, we introduce a frame-wise message design together with a Temporal Matching Module (TMM), which recovers frame correspondence under temporal reordering without requiring length-specific watermark layouts. Experiments on ModelScope and I2VGen-XL show that VideoMark achieves accurate watermark extraction on clean generations while maintaining video quality comparable to watermark-free generation. The proposed temporal matching mechanism further improves recovery under frame reordering and enables systematic evaluation under a range of temporal and compression perturbations. We additionally analyze the computational characteristics and practical operating conditions of inversion-based extraction. Overall, VideoMark provides a simple training-free construction for studying pseudorandom watermarking in videos generated by frame-aligned 2D-VAE diffusion

b9259564d42db49525a401f1.title_original: LLM-Based Website Classification for Targeted Web Measurements
b9259564d42db49525a401f1.excerpt: arXiv:2510.08101v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Web measurements based on top lists of popular websites are a well-established methodology for assessing the security and privacy landscape of the Internet. However, existing top lists are unlabeled and lack semantic information about the nature of the included websites, forcing researchers to rely on custom techniques to focus on specific website classes of interest. This makes targeted web measurements, e.g., over shopping websites, challenging to carry out. In this paper, we investigate the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to enable targeted web measurement studies. Building on prior literature, we identify key website classification tasks relevant to web measurements and highlight limitations in state-of-the-art classification approaches. We thus construct more carefully curated datasets to evaluate different LLMs on these tasks using standard performance measures. Our results show that LLMs can achieve strong performance across multiple classification scenarios, but the choice of the model and its configuration play a significant role in both the quality and the efficiency of the classification process. Finally, we use LLMs to emulate the setup of a targeted web measurement by automatically detecting adult websites in a subset of the Tranco list, without any need for custom techniques for dataset construction. Together, our benchmark evaluation and case study show that LLMs can enable high-quality targeted web measur

87b829920d718e80d13e54cf.title_original: zk-Agreements: A Privacy-Preserving Way to Establish Deterministic Trust in Confidential Agreements
87b829920d718e80d13e54cf.excerpt: arXiv:2510.20007v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Digital transactions currently exceed trillions of dollars annually, yet traditional paper-based agreements remain a bottleneck for automation, enforceability, and dispute resolution. Natural language contracts introduce ambiguity, require manual processing, and lack computational verifiability, all of which hinder efficient digital commerce. Computable legal contracts, expressed in machine-readable formats, offer a potential solution by enabling automated execution and verification. Blockchain-based smart contracts further strengthen enforceability and accelerate dispute resolution; however, current implementations risk exposing sensitive agreement terms on public ledgers, raising serious privacy and competitive intelligence concerns that limit enterprise adoption. We introduce zk-agreements, a protocol designed to transition from paper-based trust to cryptographic trust while preserving confidentiality. Our design combines zero-knowledge proofs to protect private agreement terms, secure two-party computation to enable private compliance evaluation, and smart contracts to guarantee automated enforcement. Together, these components achieve both privacy preservation and computational enforceability, resolving the fundamental tension between transparency and confidentiality in blockchain-based agreements.

1957af40c51e5b3983516407.title_original: FlowSteer: Prompt-Only Workflow Steering Exposes Planning-Time Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
1957af40c51e5b3983516407.excerpt: arXiv:2605.11514v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models (LLMs) increasingly adopt planner--executor architectures, where planners convert prompts into subtasks, roles, dependencies, and routing paths. This flexibility enables adaptive coordination, but exposes an attack surface in workflow formation: prompts can shape agent organization without modifying MAS infrastructure. We study this risk through social influence probing workflows to identify high-impact subtasks and malicious-signal propagation. The analysis reveals two vulnerabilities: workflow position can amplify or suppress a malicious signal, and sycophantic framing makes downstream agents more likely to relay it. We translate these findings into FlowSteer, a prompt-only workflow steering attack that converts vulnerability priors into one crafted prompt. FlowSteer aligns a malicious signal with influential task components and guides replanning toward dependencies that preserve propagation. Experiments show that FlowSteer increases malicious success by up to 55% over naive prompting, transfers across MAS setups, and remains effective with black-box topology inference. As FlowSteer biases the planning signals that generate the workflow, MAS defenses that inspect only the generated workflow provide limited protection. As such, we introduce FlowGuard, an input-side defense that reduces malicious success by up to 34% while preserving prompt utility. Our results posit

4e5954588690080f2a7baa23.title_original: WHET: Welding Homomorphic Encryption to Accelerator Architectures
4e5954588690080f2a7baa23.excerpt: arXiv:2606.11541v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computations on encrypted data without decryption, offering strong data privacy at the expense of substantial computational and memory overheads. Prior efforts have steadily improved FHE performance through cryptographic and algorithmic enhancements or hardware acceleration, yet these two directions have progressed largely in isolation, hindering the full exploitation of available hardware capabilities. This work presents WHET, which introduces memory-centric, architecture-aware optimizations to better align cryptographic and algorithmic constructions with FHE accelerators. We first identify conventional FHE constructions as major sources of excessive working sets and heavy off-chip memory traffic. We propose accelerator-specific algorithmic techniques, including fine-grained coefficient-to-slot transformation, plaintext compression, and intermediate modulus raising, to reduce the on-chip data footprint by minimizing temporary ciphertexts and plaintext loads. With these techniques applied, we unveil additional opportunities to improve on-chip memory efficiency; we introduce lightweight architectural refinements, including a special-purpose buffer and functional unit extensions. With these optimizations, WHET achieves 1.38--8.74$\times$ per-area performance improvements over state-of-the-art FHE accelerators and the first-ever sub-millisecond CKKS bootstrapping.

243263781ef563995439e299.title_original: WoE Wrote It? Watermarking Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Black-Box Text Provenance
243263781ef563995439e299.excerpt: arXiv:2608.29151v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) watermarks provide a mechanism for text provenance, enabling model owners to identify machine-generated content and attribute it to a specific watermarked model. However, current LLM watermarking approaches predominantly rely on inference-time sampler methods and focus their analysis on dense models. Inference-time methods are only effective when the text is explicitly generated via the model owner's controlled API; they fail in a post-theft scenario. An adversary who steals or leaks the model weights gains complete control over inference and can simply run an unmodified sampler, bypassing the watermark and preventing post-theft attribution. In this work, we introduce Watermarking of Experts (WoE), a novel black-box text provenance method that leverages the unique structural properties of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. WoE biases the vocabulary of a few secret experts, and defenders detect it by replaying suspect text through their own checkpoint to recover where these experts acted. This approach ensures the watermark remains intrinsic to the model parameters, enabling defenders to attribute text generated by stolen weights, leaked checkpoints, and secondary dense models distilled from the stolen model without needing access to the adversary's deployment or weights. We evaluate WoE across eight MoE models, demonstrating successful watermark detection from suspect text, achieving an averag

2dade55e09809a043107e4ee.title_original: Maverick: Private and Verifiable LLM Inference Made Practical via Matrix-Vector Multiplication Delegation
2dade55e09809a043107e4ee.excerpt: arXiv:2609.10264v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Open-source large language models (LLMs) are increasingly competitive with closed-source models while offering transparency and the ability to run inference without exposing user inputs to a service provider. However, running large-scale models locally requires substantial computational resources. In practice, users may still resort to a third-party provider, giving rise to privacy and correctness concerns. Existing solutions that address these problems often impose substantial server overhead or introduce additional trust assumptions. In this paper, we present Maverick, a novel approach to private and verifiable LLM inference based on a protocol for delegating matrix-vector multiplication, a dominant operation in LLMs. At its core, Maverick provides, to our knowledge, the first information-theoretically sound verification protocol for matrix-vector multiplication delegation with transparent preprocessing, efficient (batch) verification, and virtually no server overhead. We combine this verification primitive with LPN-based pseudorandom masking to provide input privacy. We implement Maverick and evaluate both of its modes on large open-source models. When only verification is required, Maverick lets commodity clients use models far beyond their own capacity: a laptop and a desktop with a 16 GB GPU generate tokens 81-270$\times$ faster on Qwen3-32B than with local inference, and reach 7-33 tokens per second on Llama 4, a 400B

224fe636566562c59cb46b04.title_original: On the Complexity of Symmetric Boolean Functions in Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages
224fe636566562c59cb46b04.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21216v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM), also known as Decomposable Randomized Encoding (DRE) or information-theoretic garbling, is a model for non-interactive secure computation. Each party encodes its input using shared randomness and sends a message to an evaluator who must recover the function output without learning anything else about the inputs. Perfect privacy requires identical transcript distributions on inputs with the same output. We also study the weaker notion of support privacy, which requires only that these distributions have the same support. We study the communication complexity of symmetric Boolean functions when each of the n parties holds one input bit. Lower bounds. We prove a $(1-o(1))n\log n$ lower bound for support-private PSM protocols computing $OR_n$, which is known to be tight. As a consequence, we obtain the same lower bounds for $MAJ_n$ and $EMAJ_n$. We also prove an $\Omega(n\log q)$ lower bound for $MOD_q$. An alternative proof technique recovers most of these bounds as well as the previously known approach based on Nechiporuk's method. Upper bounds. We construct perfectly private and support private PSM protocols of total communication $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ and $\widetilde{O}(n)$ respectively for every symmetric Boolean function, improving on the known quadratic bound. For $MAJ_n$, known branching-program constructions yield an upper bound of $O(n\log^3 n\log\log n)$. For $EMAJ_n$

dbedd273594bbf930b8556b7.title_original: SPARSEBLEED: Bypassing Attribute-Inference Defenses via Sparsity Optimizations
dbedd273594bbf930b8556b7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.38110v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a model trained on sensitive records is exposed through a prediction API, an attribute-inference attack (AIA) plugs each possible value of a missing field into a partially known record to infer which value belonged to the training record. Current defenses mask confidence scores and hide internal activations. We show that sparsity optimizations, software and hardware routines (sparse kernels) that skip arithmetic and memory fetches on zero activations or weights, reopen attribute inference through the execution footprint. We introduce SparseBleed, the first hardware and execution-based AIA on training data. Training makes neuron firing selective to sensitive attributes, so each candidate value activates a different set of neurons and sparse kernels skip the rest; the candidate value therefore sets how many multiply-accumulate operations execute and which weight columns are read, shifting response time and shared-hardware contention even when only a class label is returned. SparseBleed calibrates each candidate's footprint against reference measurements for that value. Across 11 CPU and GPU sparse libraries (e.g., Intel oneDNN-AMX, NVIDIA cuSPARSE), MLPs, and FT-Transformers up to 1.5B parameters, execution time on TACO varies by up to ~25,000 timer ticks across prediction-confidence levels. 73af23d8318cff2c37c7636b.title_original: Fault Injection Attacks on Q-Learning: Analysis, Vulnerabilities, and Countermeasures
73af23d8318cff2c37c7636b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16151v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hardware fault injection attacks threaten machine learning systems, yet their impact on reinforcement learning (RL) has received little attention despite the use of RL in safety-critical applications. This paper presents a security analysis of Q-Learning implementations under voltage and clock glitching attacks on a ChipWhisperer platform, evaluating five variants: Standard, Robust, Resilient, Linear, and Deep Q-Learning. In standard Q-Table implementations, faults corrupt reward computation, action selection, and Q-value updates during learning, and change the selected action during inference. Robust Q-Learning does not prevent these attacks: NaN and infinite values injected during learning persist in the Q-table, and its greedy policy uses the same code as standard Q-Learning. This paper also evaluates a Resilient Q-Learning variant that applies triple modular redundancy with majority voting. It corrects corruption of a single Q-table copy, but inputs shared by the copies, such as the reward, and the voting code itself remain outside its protection. The analysis extends to Linear and Deep Q-Learning, where faults corrupt stored weights during learning and change actions during inference. caad0bf6809497f60329e3c7.title_original: Anonymous in Name Only: A Critical Review and a Reidentification Exercise on the European Commission's Anonymization Measures for Google Search Data under Article 6(11) of the DMA
caad0bf6809497f60329e3c7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.17012v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In July 2026, the European Commission (EC) set out the anonymization measures Alphabet must implement to share Google Search data with competing search engines under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act. As the first concrete illustration of how the EC operationalizes anonymization under the EU digital rulebook, this methodology could become a regulatory benchmark. In this paper, we show why it should not. We critically review the anonymization measures proposed by the EC, from the characterization of residual risk to the suppression thresholds and the reliance on contractual safeguards. For each of those issues, we highlight significant conceptual flaws, and, where applicable, we illustrate these flaws with empirical observations from real Google Search data provided by Alphabet and protected under the EC's measures. Importantly, we present examples of low-effort reidentification, record linkage, and confidential attribute inference achieved through straightforward and automatable attack patterns. Our findings show that the approach of the EC relies on unjustified heuristics rather than formal privacy guarantees, underestimates the risks inherent in free-text search queries, and sacrifices data utility without achieving meaningful protection. We also demonstrate that the proposed measures do not meet any of the three anonymization criteria established by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB): no record isolation, no

1a1a5016001cf76544305dac.title_original: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Migration
1a1a5016001cf76544305dac.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25663v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. 1d9eaef38d6510850055739d.title_original: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing
1d9eaef38d6510850055739d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25809v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.

369afe11281802fbb28db89f.title_original: RAVEN: A Self-RAG Based Agent for Threat Classification and Response
369afe11281802fbb28db89f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25832v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infrastructure. We implement an early-stage prototype and report preliminary results on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads each (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; an evaluation on IDS- generated alerts and a user study are ongoing and outlined as remaining work.

b950bb549aa5e900bb5a8854.title_original: Lightweight Detection and Model Attribution of Synthetic Speech via Residual Statistical Fingerprints
b950bb549aa5e900bb5a8854.excerpt: arXiv:2411.14013v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As speech generation technologies advance, so do risks of impersonation, misinformation, and spoofing. We present a lightweight, training-free method for synthetic speech detection and source model attribution. Our method builds on model-specific fingerprints that are computed as the average of the differences between audio signals and their filtered versions, referred to as residuals. Leveraging the Mahalanobis distance of the residual for a given audio signal to these model-specific fingerprints allows to identify the source model as well as to distinguish real from fake audio. A broad set of experiments across multiple synthesis systems and languages demonstrate a supreme performance of the proposed approach on four tasks: open-world single-model attribution, closed-world multi-model attribution, real vs. synthetic speech classification, and out-of-domain detection.

0b58c0827cf37d8e88e95e65.excerpt: arXiv:2505.14914v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce the Sei Giga, a multi-concurrent producer parallelized execution EVM layer one blockchain. In an internal testnet Giga has achieved >5 gigagas/sec throughput and sub 250ms finality. Giga uses Autobahn for consensus with separate DA and consensus layers requiring f+1 votes for a PoA on the DA layer before consensus. Giga reaches consensus over ordering and uses async block execution and state agreement to remove execution from the consensus bottleneck.

b928c492131e36c030cded0c.title_original: MARGIN: Margin-Aware Regularized Geometry for Imbalanced Vulnerability Detection
b928c492131e36c030cded0c.excerpt: arXiv:2605.10240v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Software vulnerability detection is critical for ensuring software security and reliability. Despite recent advances in deep learning, real-world vulnerability datasets suffer from two severe challenges: frequency imbalance and difficulty imbalance. We reinterpret these challenges from an embedding geometry perspective, observing that such imbalances induce geometric distortions in hyperspherical representation space. To address this issue, we propose MARGIN, a metric-based framework that learns discriminative vulnerability representations through adaptive margin metric learning and hyperspherical prototype modeling. MARGIN dynamically adjusts geometric regularization according to the distribution structure estimated by the von Mises-Fisher concentration, aligning the probability mass of embedding distributions with their corresponding Voronoi cells, thereby reducing geometric distortion and yielding more stable decision boundaries. Extensive experiments on public vulnerability datasets show that MARGIN consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving notable improvements in classification and detection, especially on challenging, imbalanced datasets. Further analysis demonstrates that MARGIN produces more structured embedding geometries, improving robustness, interpretability, and generalization.

ed3c43704502ef28f408ee99.title_original: Control and Cryptosystem Co-Design for Encrypted Nonlinear Multi-Agent Coordination
ed3c43704502ef28f408ee99.excerpt: arXiv:2606.07375v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A cloud that must not see the agents' states can steer them on data encrypted under CKKS, the approximate scheme for real-valued arithmetic. Its stored estimate admits only so many multiplications before a refresh that costs time and error, and every decrypted command is flooded with noise of a mandated size, constraints no controller designed in exact arithmetic meets. For networked agents with polynomial dynamics, we prove one closed-loop bound tying the controller and the cryptosystem in both directions. If the exact loop contracts on a region, the encrypted loop stays within a certified radius of it, set by the per-cycle and refresh errors, the refresh interval, the flooding and the delay. The errors and the bound's probability are derived from the library's circuits, not measured. Inverted, the bound turns the tolerance and a failure-probability target into the refresh interval, and with it the precision, security parameters and period. Conversely, costs shape the realization: a tracing backend tallies any pipeline's operations before a ciphertext exists, and evaluating the prediction about each agent's reference holds the released error below its sixteen-agent level. A full satellite-train mission encrypted at 128-bit security ran inside its certified radius, and the certificate holds across six graphs and at 32, 64 and 128 agents. Security enters the design twice, in time and precision. The cryptosystem is there

d0c40cfb8c4882fa55fbebd1.title_original: Benchmarking Quantum Machine Learning for Power-System Attack Detection: Evaluation Choices Can Decide the Outcome
d0c40cfb8c4882fa55fbebd1.excerpt: arXiv:2608.15617v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum machine learning is proposed to detect grid cyberattacks, but no study we could read tests quantum and classical detectors under white-box, transfer, and black-box attacks and random label flips in one protocol. We compare two quantum and six classical detectors on public grid-attack data under equal tuning budgets. Our main finding: evaluation choices can decide the outcome. On these data, seven choices each changed a reported result with model families fixed. Row-level splits inflate our best score by 0.31 macro-averaged F1 over held-out files, where matched-dimensionality classical and quantum models barely clear chance. Under its own white-box attack the quantum kernel's score falls from 0.56 to 0.01 (chance 0.50), while a transferred attack in the same run leaves 0.52. Trees admit no gradient-based white-box attack, so their attacked scores are upper bounds. These attack results use eight-dimension detectors under row-level splits. On gas-pipeline and simulated-grid data, neither quantum detector is more accurate or consistently more robust; three of the seven choices reproduce fully on gas data with one pressure feature log-scaled (two within noise), and none of the four checked on the grids does. Benchmarks should hold out whole files and give every model its own attack where possible. We release code and checklist.

7767a0bb6b0bc6a22cf406de.title_original: Spectrum-Aware Bounds on Invertibility for Privacy-Enhancing Instance Encoding
7767a0bb6b0bc6a22cf406de.excerpt: arXiv:2608.23382v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Instance encoding is a popular empirical technique for privacy enhancement when sharing data to an untrusted server. It transforms sensitive data through an encoding process before sharing, with the hope that the encoding process retains utility but makes it hard to reconstruct the original data. However, most work offers no theoretical guarantee that the encoding process is actually irreversible. A recent work derived a mean-squared error (MSE) bound limiting any adversary's reconstruction accuracy, offering one of the first theoretical results in this domain. This bound, however, has three critical limitations: it is often too loose, only works with randomized encoders (excluding many deterministic encoders practitioners use), and only bounds MSE. We introduce a family of new bounds that (1) are tighter, (2) applicable even to fully deterministic encoders, and (3) can extend beyond MSE to other norm-based similarity metrics, by properly accounting for the encoder's spectral structure. We evaluate our bounds across a range of encoders, datasets, and attacks, showing they hold consistently and improve upon the existing bound.

def05c6921270af4a276cfd7.title_original: High-Throughput Private Information Retrieval with on-CPU Accelerators
def05c6921270af4a276cfd7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02376v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present AltoPIR, the first PIR system that exploits the capability of emerging on-CPU matrix accelerators such as Intel AMX. Unlike existing solutions, AltoPIR achieves high-performance PIR through efficient batching without requiring discrete accelerators. However, the on-CPU accelerator has only a few small registers and shares its core with request handling. As a result, it runs far below its peak rate while its operands arrive from memory, and it remains idle while its core handles requests. To keep the accelerator busy, we design mechanisms that reduce both the memory traffic of a batch and the core cycles spent on each request. Our experimental results show that AltoPIR outperforms existing CPU-based solutions by up to 50.1x.

669aaae20844c209ea4cbdac.title_original: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget
669aaae20844c209ea4cbdac.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16066v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A defender releases an integer-valued secret $X$ (a count, a discretised measurement, a clock value) as $Y = X + N$, where $N$ is an independent integer-valued mask whose expected absolute value, the expected distortion of the released value, is at most $c$. An adversary who knows the prior of $X$ and the law of $N$ observes $Y$ once and makes a single guess. We determine exactly how small the adversary's success probability, the posterior Bayes vulnerability, can be made, and which masks achieve it. For a secret supported on an interval of $m$ integers we give the optimum and an explicit optimiser for the uniform prior; by the maximal-leakage formula, the same mask minimises the worst-case-prior one-guess leakage for every prior with that support. For a biased bit, the simplest prior a defender can exploit, we characterise the masks that leak nothing on average, give the critical budget at which this becomes possible, and determine the entire cost-vulnerability frontier. It is the piecewise-linear interpolation of an explicit sequence of points generated by cost-optimally shifted truncated geometric masks, with infinitely many affine pieces accumulating at the critical budget, where the frontier meets the prior vulnerability with zero slope. The proof rests on a layer-cake decomposition of an arbitrary mask into truncated geometrics, along which both vulnerability and cost are exactly additive. The results give exact,

58546e6c2c9da72aacf0a55a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.20453v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis. To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. 525751e642ed0430f031b3c9.excerpt: arXiv:2611.26169v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.

c033aba3e996da788e81efee.title_ko: ShinyHunters 복귀 주장…과거 PGP 서명 확인됐지만 운영진 동일성은 불명
c033aba3e996da788e81efee.summary_ko: ShinyHunters를 자처하는 운영진이 새 Tor 유출 사이트에서 복귀를 선언하고 과거 PGP 키로 서명한 검증 메시지를 게시했다. BleepingComputer는 서명의 유효성을 확인했지만, 이는 과거 개인키에 접근할 수 있다는 뜻일 뿐 기존 운영진과 동일 인물임을 입증하지는 않는다고 설명했다. 해당 키들은 이미 폐기됐고 여러 사람이 보유했다는 소문도 있다.
c033aba3e996da788e81efee.background_ko: 관련자로 지목된 인물들의 잇단 체포 이후 기존 대표와 연락이 끊기고 유출 사이트가 중단된 가운데 새 운영진이 복귀를 주장했다.

0e976d5b5eeb5e3973749719.title_original: European Commission confirms data theft in EU Academy breach
0e976d5b5eeb5e3973749719.excerpt: The European Commission, the European Union's main executive body, has confirmed that attackers breached its EU Academy online learning hub and stole the personal data of an undisclosed number of users. [...]
0e976d5b5eeb5e3973749719.title_ko: EU 집행위, EU Academy 침해로 이용자 이름·이메일 유출 확인
0e976d5b5eeb5e3973749719.summary_ko: 유럽연합 집행위원회가 온라인 학습 플랫폼 EU Academy 침해로 이용자의 이름과 이메일 주소가 유출됐다고 확인했다. 피해 규모는 공개되지 않았으며, 집행위는 플랫폼 공개 접근을 중단하고 이용자에게 피싱성 이메일과 메시지를 주의하라고 안내했다.
0e976d5b5eeb5e3973749719.background_ko: 집행위는 AI 기반 침투 테스트 도구 ARTEX를 이용한 사이버공격을 받았다고 밝혔으며, 공격 배후는 아직 확인하지 못했다.

curation.reason_ko: 유럽연합 집행위원회가 EU Academy 침해와 이용자 개인정보 탈취를 확인했으나 피해 인원은 미공개다.

4252f119d456030bd840237e.title_original: Hackers compromise Check Point Servers in 22 organizations
4252f119d456030bd840237e.excerpt: Threat actors have exploited multiple vulnerabilities to compromise two dozen Check Point Security management servers in an ongoing campaign targeting 22 organizations. [...]
4252f119d456030bd840237e.title_ko: GreyNoise, 17개국 22개 조직의 Check Point 관리 서버 침해 포착
4252f119d456030bd840237e.summary_ko: GreyNoise는 17개국 22개 조직의 Check Point 관리 서버 24대가 침해돼 방화벽 데이터·자격증명 탈취와 보안 정책 해제 등이 이뤄졌다고 밝혔다. 초기 침입 경로와 공격 목적은 확인되지 않았다. 연구진은 자동화 양상 등을 근거로 AI 공격 도구 사용을 추정했지만, 실제 사용 여부는 확인되지 않았다.

curation.reason_ko: 진행 중인 공격에서 취약점 여러 개가 악용돼 22개 조직의 Check Point 관리 서버가 침해됐다.

7d65750683943836da03353b.title_original: From Vulnerability Noise to Resilience: Rethinking Security in the AI Era
7d65750683943836da03353b.excerpt: AI-driven development is adding complexity to software supply chains, leaving security teams overwhelmed by vulnerabilities that may pose little actual risk. RapidFort explains how runtime visibility, container hardening, and automated remediation can reduce vulnerability noise and improve software resilience. [...]
7d65750683943836da03353b.title_ko: RapidFort 전략책임자 “취약점 개수보다 실제 실행·악용 가능성에 집중해야”
7d65750683943836da03353b.summary_ko: RapidFort의 George Manuelian은 취약점 개수나 CVSS 점수보다 실제 실행 여부와 도달·악용 가능성을 중심으로 보안 우선순위를 정해야 한다고 주장했다. 런타임 분석으로 불필요한 구성요소를 제거하고, 검증된 기반 이미지와 자동 재빌드를 CI/CD에 통합해 소프트웨어 공급망의 공격 표면을 줄이는 접근을 제안했다.
7d65750683943836da03353b.background_ko: AI 지원 개발이 코드 생성과 외부 패키지 도입을 가속하면서, 배포 소프트웨어의 의존성과 실제 사용 구성요소를 파악하기 어려워졌다는 문제의식이 배경이다.

2272bd3015e16a4b7f859526.title_original: McDonald's Japan data breach exposes customer location information
2272bd3015e16a4b7f859526.excerpt: McDonald's Japan, the fast-food giant's Japanese subsidiary, has disclosed a data breach after attackers accessed a database containing sensitive information for users of the company's official smartphone app. [...]
2272bd3015e16a4b7f859526.title_ko: 맥도날드 일본 앱 데이터 유출…고객 위치·구매 내역 노출

6f25c07775b28ac9556046d2.title_original: New Shirudo tool uses AI to shield unpatched Linux systems from exploits
6f25c07775b28ac9556046d2.excerpt: OpenAI and Cisco launched an open-source Linux security tool named Shirudo that deploys temporary runtime protections to block vulnerability exploitation while administrators prepare and roll out patches, without restarting services. [...]
6f25c07775b28ac9556046d2.title_ko: OpenAI·Cisco, 패치 전 Linux 취약점 악용 막는 Shirudo 공개
6f25c07775b28ac9556046d2.summary_ko: OpenAI와 Cisco가 오픈소스 Linux 보안 도구 Shirudo를 공개했다. eBPF 기반 임시 보호 규칙을 서비스 재시작 없이 적용하며, AI가 규칙 개발·검증을 지원하되 배포는 사람이 통제한다. 연구진은 실행 중인 Elasticsearch를 중단하지 않고 공격을 차단했다고 밝혔지만, 커널에 영향을 줄 수 있는 규칙을 AI가 작성하는 데 대한 우려도 나왔다.
6f25c07775b28ac9556046d2.background_ko: 관리자가 패치를 준비하고 배포하는 동안에도 서비스를 재시작하지 않고 취약점 악용을 차단하도록 개발됐다.

03f361765c8648ac94ce505b.title_original: VMware Updates Patch Critical ESX, vCenter Vulnerabilities
03f361765c8648ac94ce505b.excerpt: The critical bugs include an authentication bypass in vCenter and flaws that could allow code execution on ESX hosts. The post VMware Updates Patch Critical ESX, vCenter Vulnerabilities appeared first on SecurityWeek .
03f361765c8648ac94ce505b.title_ko: Broadcom, VMware 취약점 23건 패치…ESX·vCenter 치명적 결함 포함
03f361765c8648ac94ce505b.summary_ko: Broadcom이 VMware 제품군의 취약점 23건을 수정하는 패치를 발표했다. vCenter의 인증 우회와 ESX의 호스트 코드 실행 관련 치명적 결함을 비롯해 Avi Load Balancer와 VMware Tools 문제도 포함됐다. vCenter 8.0 U3m에는 관련 수정이 이미 반영됐으며, 실제 공격 악용 여부는 공지에 언급되지 않았다.

38d9d219c70082d770e07ce5.title_original: Anthropic Expands Enterprise Safeguards for Detecting AI Misuse
38d9d219c70082d770e07ce5.excerpt: EFS helps zero-retention customers spot Claude misuse spread across many requests while keeping conversation data in their own cloud. The post Anthropic Expands Enterprise Safeguards for Detecting AI Misuse appeared first on SecurityWeek .
38d9d219c70082d770e07ce5.title_ko: Anthropic, 여러 요청의 패턴으로 AI 악용 탐지하는 EFS 공개 베타
38d9d219c70082d770e07ce5.summary_ko: Anthropic이 AI 악용 탐지 체계 Enterprise Frontier Safeguards(EFS)의 공개 베타를 발표했다. 개별로는 정상처럼 보이는 여러 요청에서 의심스러운 패턴을 찾아 악의적 사용과 운영자 의도를 벗어난 에이전트 행동을 탐지하도록 설계됐다. 대화 데이터는 고객 클라우드에 보관하고 Anthropic은 내용 대신 모니터링 메타데이터를 받는다.
38d9d219c70082d770e07ce5.background_ko: 대화 데이터 무보관 계약을 맺은 조직들이 개별 요청만 분석하는 분류기에 의존해 온 상황을 보완하기 위해 마련됐다.

curation.reason_ko: 대화 데이터를 고객 클라우드에 두면서 여러 요청에 걸친 Claude 오용을 탐지하는 기업용 보호책을 확대한다.

b2117a2c7b6e4d28bc7a4ae0.title_original: OpenAI, Cisco Unveil Open Source Tool to Shield Unpatched Linux Systems
b2117a2c7b6e4d28bc7a4ae0.excerpt: OpenAI and Cisco’s Shirudo uses AI-generated shields to block Linux exploits while patches are prepared, but it’s not yet production-ready. The post OpenAI, Cisco Unveil Open Source Tool to Shield Unpatched Linux Systems appeared first on SecurityWeek .
b2117a2c7b6e4d28bc7a4ae0.title_ko: OpenAI·Cisco, 미패치 Linux 보호용 오픈소스 Shirudo 공개
b2117a2c7b6e4d28bc7a4ae0.summary_ko: OpenAI와 Cisco가 AI 에이전트를 활용하는 오픈소스 보안 플랫폼 Shirudo를 공개했다. 두 회사는 에이전트가 eBPF 기반 보호 규칙을 생성·시험해 시스템 재시작 없이 취약점 악용을 차단하도록 설계했다고 설명했다. 특정 Linux 커널 기능과 추가 패치, TPM 2.0이 필요한 사전 출시 단계로, 아직 운영 환경에는 적합하지 않다.
b2117a2c7b6e4d28bc7a4ae0.background_ko: AI로 취약점 발견과 악용이 빨라지면서 패치 적용 압박이 커지자, 영구 패치를 설치하기 전 임시 보호를 제공하기 위해 개발됐다.

curation.reason_ko: 패치 전 Linux 보호용 오픈소스 도구를 공개했지만 아직 운영 환경에 투입할 단계는 아니라고 전했다.

02cd762d370e65efafe4ce3c.title_ko: Elecbrakes 블루투스 취약점, 인증 없이 트레일러 제동 조작 가능
02cd762d370e65efafe4ce3c.summary_ko: Element Digital 연구진은 Elecbrakes의 EB2·VM1·ELBC 2000에서 블루투스 범위 내 공격자가 인증 없이 트레일러 제동을 조작할 수 있음을 시연했다. EB2·VM1 패치는 배포됐으며 ELBC 2000은 대응 방안을 마련 중이다. 악용 증거는 없고, 펌웨어 변조를 통한 지속 장악 가능성은 실증하지 않은 이론적 위험이라고 연구진은 밝혔다.

curation.reason_ko: 주변 공격자가 트레일러 제동을 강제로 작동시킬 수 있다는 취약점으로 물리적 안전과 연결된다.

327951be6aabba295a801e5a.title_original: Machine-Generated Fake Plugin Turns WordPress Sites Into JavaScript Delivery Points
327951be6aabba295a801e5a.excerpt: The Wordfence Threat Intelligence Team recently analyzed a malware campaign that installs a fake WordPress plugin built almost entirely by a name generator. Various identifiers in the project – the plugin title, its directories and files, its PHP functions, variables and REST namespaces – are a machine-made compound of a prefix, a technology word and a suffix: trijavascriptly , ultravueal , maxdataic-quaddatasion . Behind the generated names is a second-stage delivery platform that runs arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of every anonymous visitor to an infected site, routes that traffic through the victim’s own domain, and lies dormant for logged-in users. In addition to files following this naming pattern, the plugin also contains files with randomized 8-character long names. We first recovered this malware during two incident response engagements, in January 2026 and September 2026. Those two malware cleanups are the source of this technical analysis. Two malware detection signatures were developed and released after undergoing our QA process on October 16, 2026. All Wordfence Premium , Wordfence Care , and Wordfence Response customers received these signatures immediately. Users of the free version of Wordfence received these signatures on November 15, 2026. As part of our product lineup, we offer security monitoring and malware removal services for our Wordfence Care and Wordfence Response customers. 327951be6aabba295a801e5a.title_ko: 가짜 WordPress 플러그인, 비로그인 방문자에 악성 JavaScript 전달
327951be6aabba295a801e5a.summary_ko: Wordfence는 자동 생성된 이름과 불필요한 코드로 위장한 가짜 WordPress 플러그인 악성코드를 분석했다. 이 플러그인은 비로그인 방문자의 브라우저에서 임의의 JavaScript를 실행하도록 하며, 로그인한 사용자에게는 작동하지 않는다. 분석팀은 서버 측 정보 탈취 코드는 발견하지 않았고 관련 탐지 서명을 배포했다고 밝혔다.

f227832c9e17936d119da406.title_original: How to compare MDR providers when every proposal looks promising
f227832c9e17936d119da406.excerpt: Choosing a managed detection and response (MDR) provider means committing budget, connecting systems, and trusting another team to act when your organization is under pressure. Yet a proposal promising 24x7 coverage, expert analysts, and fast response can leave important questions unanswered. Which systems will actually be monitored? What will analysts investigate before contacting you? What happens when an incident needs more work? Before choosing a provider or renewing your current agreement, ask for evidence of how the service operates. Rapid7’s MDR Evaluation Scorecard gives you 18 checks to structure that conversation and record what still needs proving. Start with one investigation Ask a provider to walk you through a completed investigation, using an anonymized example where necessary. Follow the initial signal through the evidence considered, the analyst’s decision, and any response actions. Suppose suspicious activity involves an account with access to a critical business system. Can the provider show how the account’s permissions, the systems within reach, and known weaknesses influenced its investigation? Can it explain what it ruled out and why it escalated or contained the activity? This exercise helps you assess whether exposure context, intelligence, and customer telemetry work together. ad1bd75bf40415d0546cebb3.title_original: Rapid7 Analysis: VMware vCenter SRP Authentication Bypass to Root (CVE-2026-123890)
ad1bd75bf40415d0546cebb3.excerpt: Overview An unauthenticated attacker can retrieve the session key for an in-progress administrator login to VMware vCenter's directory service. The attacker then uses that key to complete the login without knowing the account's password. The vulnerable interface is exposed through DCE/RPC on TCP port 2012. The issue, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 , combines a Secure Remote Password (SRP) session-key getter that is callable before authentication with an RPC context lookup that does not enforce ownership. The context handles use predictable UUIDv1 values. By creating two reference contexts around a pending login, an attacker can narrow the hidden login handle to a short timestamp window and ask the server for its key. We reproduced the bypass against vCenter Server Appliance 8.0.2.00400, build 23929136 , running Photon OS 4.0, and leveraged the resulting administrator connection through to root command execution. SSH and Bash access were initially disabled. The attack recovered the directory database and its Security Token Service (STS) signing key, forged an administrator API session, and used appliance administration features to create an account and enable SSH. Neither the existing SSO password nor the root password was an input to that chain. Impact The attacker needs network access to TCP 2012 and the name of an existing SSO principal. CVE-2026-116225.description: Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in the BER decoder in Erlang/OTP snmp allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust CPU via an SNMP message that contains an OBJECT IDENTIFIER with a very long sub-identifier. snmp_pdus:dec_oid_element/3 does not limit the number of base-128 octets in a sub-identifier, and snmp_pdus:dec_oid_elements/3 does not limit the number of sub-identifiers, so one sub-identifier can span the whole datagram. When the value exceeds the native integer size, each further octet copies a growing bignum, and decoding time grows quadratically with the sub-identifier length. The agent and the manager decode OIDs before they check community strings or SNMPv3 credentials, inside the single network interface process (snmpa_net_if or snmpm_net_if). That process does not read the next datagram until decoding completes. This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.20, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.1.3, corresponding to snmp from 4.25.1 before 5.18.2.3, 5.20.2.4, and 5.20.7. Whether OTP before OTP 17.0, corresponding to snmp before 4.25.1, is affected is unknown.

CVE-2026-116293.description: Out-of-bounds Write vulnerability in the external term format decoder in Erlang OTP erts allows an attacker who controls the input to binary_to_term/1,2 to abort the Erlang VM via a NEWER_REFERENCE_EXT term with a zero-length ID. decoded_size in erts/emulator/beam/external.c accepts a reference whose 16-bit Len field is zero, but dec_term always reads one ID word. dec_term then runs 4 bytes ahead of the position that decoded_size validated. It decodes the bytes that follow as terms that were never sized, and writes past the reserved process heap. The abort takes down every process on the node. Supervision, try/catch and the safe option do not prevent it. enif_binary_to_term() and the distribution protocol reach the same decoder, and distribution is assumed to run on trusted networks only. NEW_REFERENCE_EXT also accepts a zero length, but its range check on the first ID word rejects the shifted input. On 32-bit builds, a zero-length reference of either type at the end of the input, followed by trailing bytes, can write one word past the reserved heap. This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.20, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.1.3, corresponding to erts from 6.0 before 15.2.7.15, 16.4.0.8, and 17.1.2. Whether OTP before OTP 17.0, corresponding to erts before 6.0, is affected is unknown.

CVE-2026-116295.description: Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences in HTTP Headers ('HTTP Request/Response Splitting') vulnerability in Erlang OTP inets (httpc module) allows HTTP Request Splitting. httpc writes request header names and values to the wire without neutralizing CR, LF or NUL characters. On the default path http_request:mk_key_value_str/2, and with the headers_as_is option httpc_request:http_headers/2, build each header line by plain concatenation of the name, ": ", the value and CRLF. A CR/LF in a name or value ends the header line early. An attacker who controls data that an application puts into a header passed to httpc:request/4,5 can add or override request headers, or append a second request on the same connection. Applications that pass only constant or validated header names and values are not affected. The request line is not affected, because uri_string rejects URLs that contain raw CR/LF. This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.20, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.1.3, corresponding to inets from 5.10 before 9.3.2.9, 9.6.2.5, and 9.8.2. Whether OTP before OTP 17.0, corresponding to inets before 5.10, is affected is unknown.

CVE-2026-116382.description: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in Erlang OTP inets (httpd_script_env module) allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust the atom table of an httpd server that serves ESI scripts. When mod_esi builds the environment for an ESI callback, httpd_script_env:http_env_element/3 checks that a request header name already exists as an atom, then creates the atom http_<header-name> with list_to_atom/1. Atoms are never garbage collected, and each new atom passes the existence check on a later request. So a header named node creates http_node, a header named http_node creates http_http_node, and so on. A stream of requests to any ESI URL grows the atom table until it reaches its limit (+t), and then the whole Erlang VM aborts, together with every application on the node. This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.20, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.1.3, corresponding to inets from 5.10 before 9.3.2.9, 9.6.2.5, and 9.8.2. Whether OTP before OTP 17.0, corresponding to inets before 5.10, is affected is unknown.

CVE-2026-117642.description: Uncontrolled Recursion vulnerability in the external term format decoder in Erlang OTP erts allows an attacker who controls the input to binary_to_term/1,2 to abort the Erlang VM via a fun term with funs nested in its integer fields. dec_term in erts/emulator/beam/external.c decodes terms iteratively, except for the OldIndex and OldUniq fields of NEW_FUN_EXT and the Arity field of EXPORT_EXT. For these fields it calls itself, and it checks that the result is a small integer only after the call returns. An input that places another fun in such a field, nested to sufficient depth, recurses once per level, exhausts the stack of the scheduler thread and crashes the VM. The input must be large enough to reach that depth. The abort takes down every process on the node. Supervision, try/catch and the safe option do not prevent it. enif_binary_to_term() and the distribution protocol reach the same decoder, and distribution is assumed to run on trusted networks only. This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.20, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.1.3, corresponding to erts from 6.0 before 15.2.7.15, 16.4.0.8, and 17.1.2. Whether OTP before OTP 17.0, corresponding to erts before 6.0, is affected is unknown.

CVE-2026-119443.description: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference vulnerability in xmerl_scan in Erlang OTP xmerl allows an attacker to exhaust the memory of the Erlang VM via an XML document that names an external DTD. With default options, xmerl_scan:string/1,2 and xmerl_scan:file/1,2 fetch and parse the external DTD named in a <!DOCTYPE root SYSTEM "..."> declaration. fetch_DTD/2 in lib/xmerl/src/xmerl_scan.erl passes every system identifier to the default fetch function, which maps file: and absolute URIs to local paths, and int_file_decl/3 then reads the whole file with file:read_file/1. This happens whether or not validation is enabled, and the allow_entities option, which is false by default since OTP 27, only governs <!ENTITY> declarations and does not stop the fetch. A document naming file:///dev/zero makes the node read without bound until the operating system kills it for lack of memory, and the parse never returns. This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.20, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.1.3, corresponding to xmerl from 1.3.7 before 2.1.3.4, 2.1.9.1, and 2.2.1. Whether OTP before OTP 17.0, corresponding to xmerl before 1.3.7, is affected is unknown.

CVE-2026-120961.description: Out-of-bounds Read vulnerability in the external term format decoder in Erlang OTP erts allows an attacker who controls the input to binary_to_term/1,2 to read memory after the input, and to change one byte there, via a FLOAT_EXT term without a terminating zero byte. decoded_size in erts/emulator/beam/external.c checks only that the 31 bytes of the FLOAT_EXT field are present. dec_term then passes the field to sys_chars_to_double, which scans to a NUL byte without a length limit. When the field has no NUL, the scan continues into the bytes after the field, and those bytes change the decoded float. When the radix character is found after the field and strtod does not accept it, sys_chars_to_double overwrites that byte (a , becomes a .). The VM can fault if the scan reaches an unmapped page. The safe option does not prevent this. enif_binary_to_term() and the distribution protocol reach the same decoder, and distribution is assumed to run on trusted networks only. The write is limited to the one radix byte. No arbitrary write or code execution was shown. This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.20, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.1.3, corresponding to erts from 6.0 before 15.2.7.15, 16.4.0.8, and 17.1.2. Whether OTP before OTP 17.0, corresponding to erts before 6.0, is affected is unknown.

CVE-2026-124286.description: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature vulnerability in Erlang OTP ssl (ssl_handshake module) allows an on-path attacker to impersonate any server to a TLS 1.2 or DTLS client. When a server sends no Certificate message and a ServerKeyExchange without a signature, ssl_handshake:decode_server_key/3 reports the signature algorithm as anon, and ssl_handshake:verify_signature/5 returns true for anon without a public key. The client does not require a certificate for a certificate-authenticated key exchange, so the handshake completes for the ecdhe_rsa, ecdhe_ecdsa, dhe_rsa and dhe_dss key exchanges with a cipher suite the client offered. Certificate path validation, verify_fun and the hostname check do not run, and ssl:connect/3 returns {ok, Socket} with {verify, verify_peer} set. The TLS 1.3 client is not affected. This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.14, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.0.3, corresponding to ssl from 5.3.4 before 11.2.12.10, 11.6.0.8, and 11.7.3.
CVE-2026-124286.summary_ko: Erlang OTP의 ssl 모듈에서 암호화 서명 검증 오류로 통신 경로상의 공격자가 TLS 1.2 또는 DTLS 클라이언트에 임의의 서버를 사칭할 수 있다. TLS 1.3 클라이언트는 영향을 받지 않는다.
CVE-2026-124286.background_ko: 인증서 기반 키 교환에서도 인증서를 요구하지 않고 공개키 없는 익명 서명을 유효하게 처리해 인증서 경로와 호스트명 검증이 생략된다.

CVE-2026-130411.description: Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in woylie flop allows a remote attacker to execute code on the server via a crafted pagination cursor. Flop.Cursor.decode/2 in lib/flop/cursor.ex decodes the after and before parameters with :erlang.binary_to_term/2 in :safe mode. Its check rejects functions, PIDs, ports and references, but it accepts maps, and therefore structs of any module. Flop passes the decoded values to Ecto as query parameters. A cursor value that nests an Ecto.Query.DynamicExpr struct with a DBConnection.Stream struct as its binding fails the Ecto cast. Ecto then inspects the value for the error message, the Inspect implementation enumerates the stream, and DBConnection calls the module, function and arguments in the :log option of the stream. This issue affects flop: from 0.8.0 before 0.26.7, from 0.27.0 before 0.27.3, from 0.28.0 before 0.28.1, and from 0.29.0 before 0.29.2.
CVE-2026-130411.summary_ko: woylie flop의 페이지네이션 커서 처리에 신뢰할 수 없는 데이터 역직렬화 취약점이 있습니다. 원격 공격자가 조작된 커서를 통해 서버에서 코드를 실행할 수 있습니다.
CVE-2026-130411.background_ko: 커서 역직렬화 검사가 임의 모듈의 구조체를 허용하고, Ecto의 형 변환 오류 메시지 생성 과정에서 해당 값의 처리가 함수 호출로 이어집니다.

CVE-2026-131902.description: XML Injection vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_s3 allows an attacker who controls an object version id passed to ExAws.S3.delete_multiple_objects/3 to add objects to the batch delete. delete_multiple_objects/3 in lib/ex_aws/s3.ex builds the <Delete> request body by placing each object's version between <VersionId> tags without XML escaping. A version such as v1</VersionId></Object><Object><Key>important-file</Key></Object><Object><Key>x</Key><VersionId>v2 closes the caller's object and opens new ones, so S3 deletes objects the application never listed, including other users' objects in the same bucket. This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.0.0 before 2.6.0.

CVE-2026-133555.description: Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code ('Unsafe Reflection') vulnerability in elixir-ecto db_connection allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code via a forged DBConnection.Stream or DBConnection.PrepareStream struct. The Enumerable implementations of both structs in lib/db_connection.ex run with the options stored in the struct. The :log option accepts a {module, function, arguments} tuple, which DBConnection applies. When code enumerates a forged struct, DBConnection calls the chosen function. This issue is not exploitable in db_connection alone. It is, in theory, a vulnerability of the downstream component. The root cause is a component that decodes untrusted input with :erlang.binary_to_term/2 and does not restrict which terms the result contains. The :safe option does not reject structs, and these structs contain only plain terms. Structs of other libraries can possibly lead to the same result, so a component that decodes untrusted terms stays at risk independently of db_connection. This record exists because the struct was used in attacks on such components. This issue affects db_connection: from 1.1.0 before 2.10.3.

CVE-2026-135908.description: Rapid7 Metasploit Framework versions prior to 6.5.10 are vulnerable to an uncontrolled resource consumption issue in Rex::Proto::Http::Request#normalize!. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send an HTTP request with a deeply nested path that triggers repeated rescans of the request target, causing quadratic CPU consumption and temporarily degrading the availability of any affected HTTP listener. The issue is fixed in Metasploit Framework 6.5.10

CVE-2026-136131.description: hping3 through commit 3547c76 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in display_ipopt() that allows remote attackers to overflow the static 40-byte old_rr buffer via a crafted IP Record Route option. Attackers acting as the probed host, on-path, or spoofing the target can send replies with option lengths up to 255 to hping3 running with -G/--rroute, corrupting global memory and crashing hping3.

CVE-2026-136132.description: Pangolin before 1.21.0 contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in isPathAllowed() in server/lib/pathMatch.ts that splits paths on literal slashes without percent-decoding or resolving dot segments. Unauthenticated remote attackers can send paths with encoded slashes and dot segments to match public bypass rules while backends serve protected paths.

CVE-2026-136133.description: NocoDB before 2026.10.2 contains a denial of service vulnerability in passwordForgot() that allows unauthenticated attackers to revoke a user's sessions by requesting a password reset. Attackers who know a user's email can repeatedly request resets to sign out users, including super-admins, and permanently destroy their OAuth and MCP application authorizations.

CVE-2026-136155.description: In Valkey 9.1.0 and 9.1.1, the Lua script debugger builds its command table once and caches it with a pointer to the Lua interpreter state that was current at the time. SCRIPT FLUSH ASYNC recreates the scripting engine and frees the previous interpreter state without invalidating that cache, so the next debugger command dereferences freed memory. An authenticated user who can run scripting commands can use this to reliably crash the server, and by reclaiming the freed heap chunk with attacker-controlled bytes can escalate it to control of an indirect call, which may lead to remote code execution. The fix also addresses a second use-after-free in ldbLogStackValue. Valkey 8.0.x and 8.1.x use the previous debugger and are not affected.
CVE-2026-136155.summary_ko: Valkey 9.1.0과 9.1.1의 Lua 스크립트 디버거에 해제 후 사용 취약점이 있다. 스크립트 명령 실행 권한이 있는 인증된 사용자가 서버를 중단시킬 수 있으며, 원격 코드 실행으로 이어질 수 있다.
CVE-2026-136155.background_ko: 스크립팅 엔진 재생성 시 이전 Lua 상태를 가리키는 디버거 캐시를 무효화하지 않아, 다음 디버거 명령이 해제된 메모리를 참조한다.

CVE-2026-136156.description: In Valkey before 7.2.15, 8.0.x before 8.0.12, 8.1.x before 8.1.11, 9.0.x before 9.0.7, 9.1.x before 9.1.3 and 9.2.0-rc1, running in cluster mode, clusterCreatePublishMsgBlock computes the length of the cluster bus message for a PUBLISH or SPUBLISH as a size_t but passes it to createClusterMsgSendBlock as a uint32_t. When the channel and message together exceed 4 GiB, the length is truncated, a buffer far smaller than the message is allocated, and the full channel and message are then copied into it. An authenticated user who can publish, for example by building the arguments in a script, can overflow the heap with attacker-controlled bytes. This reliably crashes the server and may lead to remote code execution. Servers that do not run in cluster mode are not affected.
CVE-2026-136156.summary_ko: 클러스터 모드로 실행되는 Valkey의 일부 버전에 정수 잘림으로 인한 힙 버퍼 오버플로 취약점이 있다. 메시지 게시 권한이 있는 인증된 사용자가 서버를 중단시킬 수 있으며, 원격 코드 실행으로 이어질 수 있다.
CVE-2026-136156.background_ko: 클러스터 메시지 길이를 size_t에서 uint32_t로 전달할 때 4 GiB를 넘는 길이가 잘려 작은 버퍼가 할당되고, 여기에 전체 데이터가 복사된다.

CVE-2026-136157.description: In Valkey 8.0.x before 8.0.11, 8.1.x before 8.1.10, 9.0.x before 9.0.6 and 9.1.x before 9.1.2, the RDMA transport's pending-data handler walks its connection list with an iterator that caches the next entry. A command processed from inside that loop, such as CLIENT KILL, can synchronously free another client's connection, and closing an RDMA connection did not remove it from the pending list, so the handler then uses freed memory. An authenticated user can use this to reliably crash the server, and the freed heap chunk can be reclaimed with attacker-influenced bytes. Only servers built with RDMA support (USE_RDMA) and configured with an RDMA listener are affected.

CVE-2026-136158.description: In Valkey JSON 1.0.0 through 1.0.2, a recursive JSONPath expression such as $..* returns both an array and elements nested inside it. The size-changing mutators (JSON.ARRAPPEND, JSON.ARRINSERT, JSON.ARRPOP, JSON.ARRTRIM and JSON.CLEAR) process the ancestor first, which can reallocate its element buffer and free the old storage while the descendant entries in the result set still point into it; the module then writes through those dangling pointers. An authenticated user who can run these commands can use this to reliably crash the server, and it has been developed into remote code execution as the user the server runs as. Servers that do not load the JSON module, including through valkey-bundle, are not affected.
CVE-2026-136158.summary_ko: Valkey JSON 1.0.0~1.0.2에 해제 후 사용 취약점이 있다. 관련 명령 실행 권한이 있는 인증된 사용자가 서버를 중단시키거나 서버 실행 계정 권한으로 원격 코드를 실행할 수 있으며, JSON 모듈을 로드하지 않은 서버는 영향받지 않는다.
CVE-2026-136158.background_ko: 재귀 JSONPath 결과의 상위 배열 변경으로 요소 버퍼가 재할당·해제될 때 하위 요소의 포인터가 남아 있어 해제된 메모리에 쓰기가 발생한다.

CVE-2026-136159.description: TypiCMS Core before 17.0.46 contains an insufficiently protected credentials vulnerability that allows authenticated users with "read users" permission to view plaintext api_token values for all users, including superusers, via the GET /api/users endpoint. Attackers can steal a superuser's non-expiring, non-rotatable api_token from the JSON response and use it to gain full superuser API access, enabling creation and deletion of users, roles, and all content.

CVE-2026-136160.description: Pyro through 1.9.2 contains an insecure deserialization vulnerability in ParamStoreDict.load() that calls torch.load with weights_only=False, unpickling arbitrary Python objects. Attackers can trick users into loading a crafted parameter file defining __reduce__ to execute code with the privileges of the Python process.

CVE-2026-136165.description: Fider before 0.40.0 contains an account takeover vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to sign in as existing users by linking OAuth identities through unverified email matches. Attackers can use a Google account carrying an unverified copy of a victim's email, including a tenant administrator's, to bind their identity via the OAuthToken handler and obtain persistent session access.

CVE-2026-136166.description: Wallabag from 2.0.0-beta.1 before 2.6.16 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated users to annotate other users' entries by referencing global entry IDs. Attackers can send requests to the /annotations/{entry} or /api/annotations/{entry} routes to inject annotations into victims' private entries, API output, and exports, and enumerate existing entry IDs.

CVE-2026-136167.description: vedo through 2026.6.3 contains an insecure deserialization vulnerability that allows attackers to execute code by supplying crafted .npy or .npz files loaded with allow_pickle=True. Attackers can embed an object with a malicious __reduce__ method in mesh, assembly, scene or font files to run code with the victim's privileges when opened.

CVE-2026-136168.description: RedVector before 8.1.0 contains a hard-coded credentials vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to execute commands by supplying the default redvector-dev-token bearer token. Attackers can call /api/python/execute or /api/process/execute-async to run Python scripts and commands as the server user, even via malicious web pages abusing permissive CORS against loopback instances.

CVE-2026-136169.description: Cockpit CMS through 2.14.1 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows authenticated users with content create or update permission to inject script via unescaped linked item _id values. Attackers can save an item whose link _id contains a double quote and HTML markup, executing script when administrators view the content dashboard or collection list.

CVE-2026-136170.description: Assimp through 6.0.6 contains a use-after-free and double free vulnerability in OpenGEXImporter.cpp because InternReadFile does not reset cached importer state between files. Attackers can supply OpenGEX files to applications reusing one Importer instance, causing freed node, camera, and material pointers to corrupt heap memory and crash.

CVE-2026-136171.description: Assimp through 6.0.6 contains a use-after-free vulnerability in BVHLoader.cpp that allows attackers to read freed aiNode objects because the mNodes vector is never cleared between files. Attackers can supply multiple BVH files to an application reusing one Importer instance, causing CreateAnimation to copy freed mName data into channel names, crashing the application or exposing heap contents.

CVE-2026-136172.description: Assimp through 6.0.6 contains a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the OBJ exporter that allows attackers to corrupt memory via NaN vertex components breaking comparator ordering. Attackers can supply a crafted PLY file with NaN texture coordinates or vertex colors that, when exported to OBJ in libc++ builds, writes file-controlled data past a heap buffer and crashes the application.

CVE-2026-62273.description: XML Injection vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_s3 allows an attacker who controls tag keys or values to inject forged tag entries into S3 object and bucket tagging requests. ExAws.S3.put_object_tagging/4 and ExAws.S3.put_bucket_tagging/2 in lib/ex_aws/s3.ex build the <TagSet> request body by interpolating tag keys and values directly into <Key> and <Value> elements via to_string/1, without applying the module's existing escape_xml_string/1 helper (which delete_multiple_objects already uses for object keys). An application that forwards user-supplied data as a tag key or value lets an attacker close the intended element and inject attacker-chosen <Tag> entries. For example, a tag value of blue</Value></Tag><Tag><Key>owner</Key><Value>admin turns one intended tag into two tags on the wire. Because S3 honors tags in access-control conditions (aws:RequestTag, s3:ExistingObjectTag) and cost-allocation reporting, an injected tag can forge an authorization-relevant tag or corrupt the intended tag set. This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.0.2 before 2.6.0.

CVE-2026-63581.description: XML Injection vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_s3 (ExAws.S3 module) allows an attacker to inject arbitrary XML configuration elements into S3 bucket-configuration request bodies via unescaped, caller-supplied values. This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/ex_aws/s3.ex and program routines ExAws.S3.put_bucket_logging/2, ExAws.S3.put_bucket_notification/2, ExAws.S3.put_bucket_replication/2, ExAws.S3.put_bucket_website/2. The bucket-configuration body builders construct their XML by interpolating caller-supplied values directly into the request body without escaping, and never route them through the module's own escape_xml_string/1 helper. A value containing XML metacharacters (<, >, &, quotes) can close the intended element early and open attacker-chosen elements, which the builder's trailing closing tag then closes, keeping the document single-rooted and well-formed. In a multi-tenant application where tenants configure their own bucket settings, an attacker who can influence one of the interpolated field values (for example the logging target, a notification ARN, a replication destination or Account, or a website redirect HostName) can inject arbitrary configuration nodes into a request the application signs and sends to AWS. The affected builders are reached through the public functions put_bucket_logging/2, put_bucket_notification/2, put_bucket_replication/2, and put_bucket_website/2. This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.5.9 before 2.6.0.

CVE-2026-63582.description: Externally Controlled Reference to a Resource in Another Sphere vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_s3 allows an attacker who controls an S3 bucket name to make presigned URLs and presigned POST forms point at a host of their choice. With virtual_host: true, s3_accelerate: true or bucket_as_host: true, ExAws.S3.presigned_url/5 and ExAws.S3.presigned_post/4 build the URL from the bucket name without checking it. A bucket such as attacker.example/x? turns the URL into https://attacker.example/x?.s3.amazonaws.com..., and the signature is computed for that host. Clients given the URL upload their files to, or download content from, the attacker's host, and every such URL discloses the access key id. With bucket_as_host: true any valid hostname works as the bucket name. This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.0.0 before 2.6.0.

CVE-2026-63583.description: ExAws.S3.Utils.build_lifecycle_rule/1 in ex_aws_s3 interpolates caller-supplied lifecycle rule fields (the rule id, filter prefix, tag key and value, storage class, and noncurrent-version count) directly into the PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration XML body without escaping XML metacharacters. An application that populates any of these fields from untrusted input (for example a tenant-supplied object tag) lets an attacker break out of the surrounding element and inject arbitrary XML into the request, including an entirely new lifecycle action such as a delete-after-one-day expiration that destroys the bucket's objects. The public entry point ExAws.S3.put_bucket_lifecycle/2 flows directly into this builder. This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.3.0 before 2.6.0.

CVE-2026-63584.description: Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences ('CRLF Injection') vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_s3 allows HTTP header injection via an attacker-controlled copy-source key. ExAws.S3.upload_part_copy/8 in lib/ex_aws/s3.ex builds the x-amz-copy-source request header by interpolating the source bucket and object key directly into "/#{src_bucket}/#{src_object}" with no percent-encoding. The sibling function put_object_copy percent-encodes the bucket and each path segment before assembling the same header, but upload_part_copy skips encoding entirely. When the source key is derived from untrusted input, reserved characters (spaces, ?, &, =) pass through verbatim and corrupt the copy-source reference, so the copy targets the wrong object or fails. A key containing \r or \n can split or inject additional headers into the outgoing HTTP request, depending on how the configured HTTP backend serializes headers. Applications that pass a source bucket or object key derived from untrusted input to ExAws.S3.upload_part_copy/8 are affected. Applications that only ever pass trusted, well-formed keys are not affected. This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.0.0 before 2.6.0.

CVE-2026-63585.description: ExAws.S3 constructs S3 ACL grant headers (such as x-amz-grant-read and x-amz-grant-full-control) in format_grant_header/1 by interpolating grantee identifiers into a quoted, comma-separated list without escaping. Grantee email and id values are wrapped in double quotes and joined with a comma, but double-quote, comma, and CR/LF characters in the value are not neutralized. An application that passes an attacker-influenced grantee value (for example an email address taken from a "share this object" feature) into an ACL grant option (grant_read, grant_write, grant_read_acp, grant_write_acp, or grant_full_control) lets the attacker close the quoted token and inject an additional grantee, such as the attacker's own canonical id or the predefined AllUsers group URI, into the header.
